opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the form factor should follow the job. Quadrupeds, the robotic dogs, are fantastic at mobility. They handle stairs, rubble, uneven terrain, and they're very stable because they've got four points of contact. That makes them great for inspection, patrolling, carrying sensors into places that are dangerous or tedious for people: walking a plant floor, checking gauges, doing thermal scans, going into a site after an incident.

But a dog can mostly look and carry. The moment you need to *do* something, like open a door with a lever handle, turn a valve, press a button on a panel, pick up a tool, or move a box off a shelf, you run into the fact that our entire built environment was designed around the human body. Door heights, stair rises, control panels, ladders, tools, vehicles: all of it assumes two arms, two hands, and a torso at roughly human height. You can bolt an arm onto a quadruped, and that helps, but it's still a compromise.

A humanoid is the bet that, instead of redesigning the world for robots, you build a robot that fits the world we already have. That's a big deal for adoption, because most customers can't rebuild their facilities to accommodate automation.

So I don't see it as one or the other. I see a team. The quadruped is your scout and your mobile sensor platform. It covers ground, gathers data, and goes where footing is bad. The humanoid is the one that shows up when there's manipulation work to be done in a space built for people. Over time I think you'll see them working together, with the dog finding the problem and the humanoid fixing it, and both feeding into the same software layer so a human operator is supervising a fleet rather than joysticking individual machines.

And honestly, it's early. Quadrupeds are much further along in terms of reliability and real deployments. Humanoids still have a lot to prove on balance, battery life, dexterity, and cost. But the reason so much energy is going into them is that the payoff, a general-purpose machine that can step into human workflows, is enormous if we get it right.

r001.rationale: The response says robotic dogs can mostly look and carry, and that manipulation tasks such as opening doors or turning valves expose limitations of the quadruped form factor.

r002.rationale: It does not compare camera placement at head height with placement in the chest.

r003.rationale: It describes a quadruped with an added arm as a compromise and explains why humanoids fit human-built spaces, but does not clearly argue that finding another form factor capable of the same breadth of physical interactions would be difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the world we've built is designed for humans, not for dogs. Every door handle, every staircase, every shelf, every tool is sized and shaped for a body with two arms, two hands, and roughly five to six feet of height. A quadruped is fantastic at mobility. It can handle rough terrain, stairs, tight spaces, and it's incredibly stable, which is why dogs have been so successful in inspection, security, and industrial environments. But the moment you need to manipulate something in a human environment, open a cabinet, carry a box from a shelf to a cart, use a tool that was designed for a hand, the dog form factor starts to run out of road. You can bolt an arm onto a dog, and people do, but you're fighting the geometry of the platform.

So I don't see it as humanoids versus dogs. I see them as complementary. The dog is the right answer when the job is "go somewhere difficult and sense or observe." The humanoid is the right answer when the job is "do the thing a person would do in a space built for people." In a factory or a warehouse or a hospital, you'll have both. The dog patrols the perimeter or inspects the piping. The humanoid works alongside people on the line or restocks the supply room, using the same workflows and the same infrastructure the humans use, without having to retrofit the building.

The other piece is training data. The human form factor lets you learn directly from human demonstration, from video, from teleoperation, in a way that transfers much more naturally than it does to a four-legged body. That's a huge accelerant. So when people ask me why bother with a humanoid when dogs already work, my answer is that dogs solved mobility. Humanoids are how we get to manipulation at scale in the environments we actually live and work in.

r001.rationale: It says the dog form factor runs out of road for manipulating objects in human environments and that attaching an arm fights the platform’s geometry.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss camera placement or compare head height with chest placement.

r003.rationale: It contrasts quadrupeds with humanoids and describes the dog’s manipulation limits, but does not state that finding any non-humanoid form with comparable breadth of physical interaction would be difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think they serve different purposes. A robotic dog is a great platform for moving through a facility, carrying sensors, and inspecting things. But once you need to open a door, turn a valve, or pick something up, you need manipulation.

The case for humanoids is that we’ve built the world around the human body. Our tools, workspaces, and equipment are designed for people with two hands. A robot that can work in that environment could take on tasks without requiring us to redesign the whole facility. So I see them as complementary: use the dog where mobility and sensing are the priority, and use a humanoid where the job requires interacting with the world in a more human way.

r001.rationale: The response says robotic dogs are suited to mobility and sensing but cannot readily open doors, turn valves, or pick things up, motivating humanoids for manipulation.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about camera placement or the usefulness of head-height versus chest-height cameras.

r003.rationale: It says humanoids fit human-designed environments, but does not argue that a non-humanoid form capable of the same breadth of physical interaction would be difficult to develop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a place for both. A robotic dog has a very stable platform, and it’s great for moving through a facility, carrying sensors, and doing inspections. But when you need to interact with the world, the humanoid form starts to make sense. We’ve built our environments around people—the doors, the stairs, the tools, the height of a workbench. A robot with arms and hands can potentially use what’s already there.

So I don’t see humanoids replacing robotic dogs. I see different platforms doing different jobs. If you need mobility and sensing, four legs may be the right answer. If you need to manipulate something or perform a task designed for a person, that’s where a humanoid could add value.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the dog’s strengths in mobility and sensing with the humanoid’s advantage for interacting with and manipulating human-oriented environments, identifying a limitation of the dog form as a reason for humanoids.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss camera placement or compare head height with chest placement.

r003.rationale: The response says humanoids can use human-oriented environments, but does not argue that another form factor would struggle to match the breadth of physical interactions a humanoid can perform.
